questions.text: A deck of cards contains 60% red cards and 40% blue cards. You must predict the color before each draw (with replacement). Over 100 draws, which strategy will give you the HIGHEST number of correct predictions?
options: Always predict red
Predict red 60 times and blue 40 times
Alternate between red and blue equally
questions.explanation: Always predicting red gives 60% success (60/100 correct). Predicting red 60 times and blue 40 times gives only ~52% success on average. The 'probability matching' error is reproducing the proportions instead of always choosing the most probable option.

questions.text: A fair coin (50-50 heads or tails) has just landed on heads five times in a row. For the sixth toss:
options: Tails is more likely to come up
Heads is more likely to come up
Heads and tails are equally probable
questions.explanation: The tosses are independent. The coin has no memory. P(heads) = P(tails) = 50% on each toss, regardless of history.

questions.text: A couple has 4 daughters. They want a fifth child. What is the probability that it will be a boy?
options: More than 50% (after 4 girls, a boy becomes more likely)
Less than 50% (they tend to have girls)
About 50% (each birth is independent)
questions.explanation: Each birth is independent. Previous births do not affect the probability of the next child (~50% boy/girl).

questions.text: Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was concerned with social discrimination. Rank by probability:
options: Linda is a teacher
Linda is a bank teller
Linda is active in the feminist movement
Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement
questions.explanation: Despite the description, P(bank teller) > P(bank teller and feminist) mathematically. This is the famous 'Linda problem': a conjunction can never be more probable than its components.

questions.text: Mark likes video games and spends a lot of time on his computer. Rank by probability:
options: Mark works in IT
Mark is a video game developer
Mark is an accountant
Mark works in IT and plays on an e-sports team
questions.explanation: P(IT) must be ranked as more probable than P(IT AND e-sports). The conjunction is always less probable.

questions.text: A disease affects 1% of the population. A test correctly detects the disease in 90% of sick people. Among healthy people, the test incorrectly shows positive in 9% of cases. If your test is positive, what is your actual probability of being sick?
questions.explanation: Out of 10,000 people: 100 are sick (90 test positive), 9,900 are healthy (891 test falsely positive). Probability of being sick = 90/(90+891) ≈ 9.2%. Many people ignore the base rate (1%) and overestimate their probability of being sick.

questions.text: In a company, 70% of employees are engineers and 30% are managers. Sophie is charismatic, loves leading teams, and excels at negotiations. Is she more likely:
options: Engineer
Manager
Impossible to determine with this info
questions.explanation: Despite the description suggesting a manager profile, the base rate (70% engineers vs 30% managers) remains the most important factor. Many engineers can also be charismatic and enjoy leading.

questions.text: A city has 2 hospitals: the large one (45 births/day) and the small one (15 births/day). About 50% of babies are boys, but it varies daily. Over a year, which hospital recorded the most days with >60% boys?
options: The large hospital
The small hospital
About the same
questions.explanation: The small hospital. Small samples have more variance. It's easier to get extremes with 15 observations than with 45.

questions.text: In college basketball, players who excel in their first year tend to perform less well in their second year. What is the best explanation?
options: They become complacent after their success
Opponents study their game and adapt
Extreme performances include luck that doesn't repeat
questions.explanation: Regression to the mean. Exceptional performances combine talent and luck. Luck doesn't persist, so performances return toward the player's average.

questions.text:
Rule to test: 'If Lyon is on one side of the ticket, then train is on the other side.'

You have 4 tickets in front of you:
• Ticket 1 shows: **Lyon**
• Ticket 2 shows: **Paris**
• Ticket 3 shows: **Car**
• Ticket 4 shows: **Train**

Which tickets would be SUFFICIENT to check to verify if the rule is respected or violated?
options: Lyon only
Lyon and Train
Lyon and Car
All tickets
Lyon, Paris and Car
questions.explanation: It's sufficient to flip Lyon (verify the other side = train) and Car (verify the other side ≠ Lyon). Train and Paris cannot violate the rule, so flipping them would be unnecessary.

questions.text:
You're checking the law: 'If a person drinks alcohol, they must be 18 years or older.'

You observe 4 people:
• Person A: **Drinking beer**
• Person B: **Drinking orange juice**
• Person C: **Is 25 years old**
• Person D: **Is 16 years old**

Who would be SUFFICIENT to check to determine if the law is respected or violated?
options: Person A only
Persons A and D
Persons A and C
All persons
Persons A, B and D
questions.explanation: You need to check person A (is they ≥18?) and person D (are they drinking alcohol?). The others cannot violate the rule, so checking them would be useless.

questions.text: Researchers found that teenagers who smoke tend to have lower IQ scores. Does this mean that preventing teens from smoking would increase their IQ?
options: Yes
No
Cannot tell
questions.explanation: Correlation ≠ causation. There may be a confounding variable (stress, socioeconomic environment, etc.).

questions.text: An unpopular school principal is defended because absenteeism dropped 12% since her appointment. What evidence would best refute this claim?
options: 40% more absences are reported in surveys than in official records
Common sense says a principal has little impact on absenteeism
Absenteeism rates in two neighboring cities dropped 18% during the same period
The superintendent had questionable business contacts
questions.explanation: Comparison with a control group (similar cities) shows the decrease is general, not due to the principal.

questions.text: Talia has finger thickening. To estimate her probability of having hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (a rare bone disease), what information is needed?
options: Only: % of people with the syndrome who have thickening
Only: % of people without the syndrome who have thickening
Both: % with syndrome who have this symptom AND % without syndrome who have this symptom
Impossible to estimate even with this information
questions.explanation: You need both rates: how many sick people have the symptom AND how many healthy people have the symptom. This allows calculating the probability of being sick given you have the symptom (Bayes' theorem).

questions.text:
Rule: 'If a product is organic, it must have certification.'

You have 4 products in front of you:
• Product 1: **Labeled organic**
• Product 2: **Labeled conventional**
• Product 3: **With certification**
• Product 4: **Without certification**

Which products would be SUFFICIENT to check to determine if the rule is respected or violated?
options: Labeled organic only
Labeled organic and With certification
Labeled organic and Without certification
All products
Labeled organic, Labeled conventional and Without certification
questions.explanation: It's sufficient to check [Organic] (does it have certification?) and [Without certification] (is it organic?). The others cannot violate the rule, so checking them would be unnecessary.

questions.text: A study shows that people who drink coffee have less heart disease. Should we recommend coffee for heart health?
options: Yes, the correlation proves the protective effect
No, we need a randomized controlled trial
Yes, if the correlation is strong
questions.explanation: A correlation does not prove causation. Coffee drinkers may have other healthy habits (exercise, diet).

questions.text: We observe that cities with more firefighters have more serious fires. Should we reduce the number of firefighters?
options: Yes, they seem to cause fires
No, the causality is reversed
Yes, if there is a real correlation
questions.explanation: Reverse causality: large cities have more fires, so they hire more firefighters. Firefighters don't cause fires.

questions.text: A new teaching technique shows +15% exam success. How to verify its effectiveness?
options: Compare with last year's results
Ask teachers' opinions
Compare with a control group that didn't get the new technique
Check if students are satisfied
questions.explanation: A control group is essential. Results may have increased for other reasons (exam difficulty, motivation, etc.).

questions.text: To test if a new drug reduces fever, which experiment is best?
options: Give the drug to feverish patients and measure temperature 2h later
Give the drug to one group and a placebo to a control group, double-blind
Ask patients if they feel better after the drug
questions.explanation: A randomized controlled double-blind trial is the gold standard for testing causal efficacy. It eliminates the placebo effect and confirmation bias.

questions.text:
Data collected over 200 days:

| Weather | Traffic jams | No traffic jams |
|---------|--------------|------------------|
| Rain | 80 days | 20 days |
| Sunny | 40 days | 60 days |

Does rain cause traffic jams?
options: Yes, 80 cases of rain with traffic
Yes, P(Traffic|Rain) = 80% > P(Traffic|Sunny) = 40%
No, no clear relationship
Impossible to say
questions.explanation: Covariation: P(T|Rain) = 80/100 = 80% vs P(T|Sunny) = 40/100 = 40%. Rain increases the probability of traffic.

questions.text: Hypothesis: 'All swans are white.' Which observation is most informative for testing this hypothesis?
options: Observe 100 white swans
Observe 1 black swan
Observe 1000 white swans
questions.explanation: Popper's falsification principle: a single counterexample (black swan) definitively refutes the hypothesis. A thousand confirmations (white swans) can never prove it with certainty.

questions.text: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
questions.explanation: 5 cents. If ball = 5c, bat = $1.05 ($1 more), total = $1.10. Intuition suggests 10c, but that would give a total of $1.20.

questions.text: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 parts, how long do 100 machines take to make 100 parts?
questions.explanation: 5 minutes. Each machine makes 1 part in 5 minutes. So 100 machines make 100 parts in 5 minutes (in parallel). Intuition suggests 100 minutes.

questions.text: In a lake, there is a water lily. Each day, its size doubles. It takes 48 days to cover the entire lake. In how many days does it cover half the lake?
questions.explanation: 47 days. If the lake is full on day 48 and the size doubles each day, then on day 47 it is half covered. Intuition suggests 24 days.

questions.text: If it takes one minute to make each cut, how long will it take to cut a 25-foot plank into 25 equal pieces?
questions.explanation: 24 minutes. It takes 24 cuts to get 25 pieces (not 25 cuts). Intuition suggests 25 minutes.

questions.text: If you are in a race and you pass the runner in second position, what position are you in now?
options: First position
Second position
Third position
questions.explanation: Second position. You take the place of the one who was 2nd. Intuition suggests 1st position.

questions.text: A farmer has 15 sheep. All but 9 die. How many are left?
questions.explanation: 9 sheep. 'All but 9' means that 9 survive. Intuition often suggests 6 (15-9).

questions.text: A book and a pen cost $12. The book costs $10 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost?
questions.explanation: $1. If pen = $1, book = $11 ($10 more), total = $12. Intuition suggests $2.

questions.text:
Evaluate only the LOGIC (not the truth in reality):

Premise 1: All mammals can walk.
Premise 2: Whales are mammals.
Conclusion: Whales can walk.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AAA1). Even if the conclusion is false in reality, it follows logically from the premises. Inconsistent syllogism (validity ≠ believability).

questions.text: Premise 1: All flowers need water. Premise 2: Roses need water. Conclusion: Roses are flowers.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Even if the conclusion is true, it doesn't follow logically from the premises. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: No reptile has fur. Premise 2: All snakes are reptiles. Conclusion: No snake has fur.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (EAE1). The conclusion follows logically from the premises and is true. Consistent syllogism (validity = believability).

questions.text: Premise 1: All birds can fly. Premise 2: Penguins are birds. Conclusion: Penguins can fly.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AAA1). The conclusion follows from the premises, even if it is false in reality. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text:
Evaluate ONLY the LOGIC (not truth in reality):

Premise 1: All plants are photosynthetic organisms.
Premise 2: All ferns are photosynthetic organisms.
Conclusion: All ferns are plants.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Even though the conclusion is true (ferns are plants), it doesn't logically follow from the premises. There could be other photosynthetic organisms that aren't plants (algae, certain bacteria). Consistent syllogism: validity ≠ believability.

questions.text: Premise 1: No mammal lays eggs. Premise 2: Platypuses lay eggs. Conclusion: Platypuses are not mammals.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (EAE2). The conclusion follows from the premises, even if it is false (platypuses are mammals). Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All fruits contain vitamins. Premise 2: Oranges are fruits. Conclusion: Oranges contain vitamins.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AAA1). The conclusion follows from the premises and is true. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All politicians are liars. Premise 2: John is a liar. Conclusion: John is a politician.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). The conclusion doesn't follow logically from the premises (there can be non-politician liars). Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Three stacked boxes: [Top: fresh strawberries], [Middle: ?], [Bottom: frozen strawberries]. Fresh strawberries must NOT touch frozen ones. Does a box of fresh strawberries touch a box of frozen strawberries?
options: Yes
No
Cannot determine
questions.explanation: Yes. If Middle = fresh, then Middle touches Bottom (frozen). If Middle = frozen, then Top (fresh) touches Middle. Either way: violation.

questions.text: Anne is looking at Paul. Paul is looking at Mary. Anne is married. Mary is not married. We don't know if Paul is married. Is a married person looking at an unmarried person?
options: Yes
No
Cannot determine
questions.explanation: Yes. If Paul is married, he's looking at Mary (unmarried). If Paul is not married, Anne (married) is looking at him. Either way: yes.

questions.text: Is the distance from San Francisco to Hawaii greater than 500 miles? What do you think is the exact distance?
questions.explanation: The real distance is ~2387 miles. To score points, you need to resist the low anchor (500). If your estimate is >1000 miles (more than 2x the anchor), you resisted the anchoring bias. This question measures resistance to anchoring, not knowledge of the correct answer.

questions.text: Is the duration of Mars' orbit around the Sun greater than 1500 days? What do you think is the exact duration?
questions.explanation: The actual duration is 687 days. To score points, you need to resist the high anchor (1500). If your estimate is <750 days (less than half the anchor), you resisted the anchoring bias. This question measures resistance to anchoring, not knowledge of the correct answer.
